Fix integers n and r with 0 <= r <= n. Then n-r is also an integer, and 0 <= n-r <= n.

By the stated definition,
[n choose r]_q = (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r}).

Since n-r is an admissible lower index as well, the same definition gives
[n choose n-r]_q = (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_{n-r} (q;q)_{n-(n-r)}) = (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_{n-r} (q;q)_r).

Now multiplication of polynomials is commutative, so
(q;q)_{n-r} (q;q)_r = (q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r}.
Therefore the two right-hand sides are identical, and hence
[n choose n-r]_q = (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r}) = [n choose r]_q.

Thus [n choose r]_q = [n choose n-r]_q. Since both sides are the Gaussian q-binomial coefficients defined by the given q-factorial formula, this is an identity of polynomials in q. This proves the claimed symmetry.

children.proof_nl:
Let G_{n,r}(q) := (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r}). Since each factor 1 - q^i is a nonzero polynomial in Z[q], each (q;q)_m is nonzero, so G_{n,r}(q) is a well-defined element of the rational function field Q(q).

We prove by induction on n that for every integer r with 0 <= r <= n, G_{n,r}(q) is a nonzero polynomial in Z[q] of degree r(n-r).

Base case n = 0: then r = 0, and
G_{0,0}(q) = (q;q)_0 / ((q;q)_0 (q;q)_0) = 1.
This is a nonzero polynomial in Z[q] of degree 0 = 0(0-0).

Induction step: assume the claim has been proved for n-1, and let r satisfy 0 <= r <= n.

If r = 0, then
G_{n,0}(q) = (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_0 (q;q)_n) = 1.
If r = n, then
G_{n,n}(q) = (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_n (q;q)_0) = 1.
In either case G_{n,r}(q) is a nonzero polynomial of degree 0 = r(n-r).

Now assume 0 < r < n. We derive the usual recurrence directly from the definition. Using
(q;q)_{n-r} = (1 - q^{n-r})(q;q)_{n-r-1}
and
(q;q)_r = (1 - q^r)(q;q)_{r-1},
we have in Q(q):

G_{n-1,r}(q)
= (q;q)_{n-1} / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r-1})
= (1 - q^{n-r})(q;q)_{n-1} / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r}),

and

q^{n-r} G_{n-1,r-1}(q)
= q^{n-r} (q;q)_{n-1} / ((q;q)_{r-1} (q;q)_{n-r})
= q^{n-r}(1 - q^r)(q;q)_{n-1} / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r}).

Adding these two identities gives

G_{n-1,r}(q) + q^{n-r} G_{n-1,r-1}(q)
= ((1 - q^{n-r}) + q^{n-r}(1 - q^r))(q;q)_{n-1} / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r})
= (1 - q^n)(q;q)_{n-1} / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r})
= (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r})
= G_{n,r}(q).

So for 0 < r < n,
G_{n,r}(q) = G_{n-1,r}(q) + q^{n-r} G_{n-1,r-1}(q).

By the induction hypothesis, both G_{n-1,r}(q) and G_{n-1,r-1}(q) are nonzero polynomials in Z[q]. Hence their sum G_{n,r}(q) also lies in Z[q].

Now compute degrees. By induction,
deg G_{n-1,r}(q) = r((n-1)-r) = r(n-r) - r,
and
deg G_{n-1,r-1}(q) = (r-1)(n-r).
Therefore

deg(q^{n-r} G_{n-1,r-1}(q)) = (n-r) + (r-1)(n-r) = r(n-r).

Since r > 0, we have
r(n-r) - r < r(n-r).
Thus the second summand has strictly larger degree than the first. Because G_{n-1,r-1}(q) is nonzero, q^{n-r} G_{n-1,r-1}(q) has a nonzero term of degree r(n-r); the first summand has no term of that degree, so no cancellation is possible. Hence

deg G_{n,r}(q) = r(n-r).
In particular G_{n,r}(q) is nonzero.

This completes the induction. Therefore for all integers n and r with 0 <= r <= n, the Gaussian q-binomial coefficient [n choose r]_q is a nonzero polynomial in Z[q] of degree r(n-r).

children.proof_nl:
Assume that the rational function A(q)/B(q) is a polynomial in Z[q]. Then there exists a polynomial C(q) in Z[q] such that

A(q)=B(q)C(q).

Because A(q) and B(q) are both nonzero, C(q) must also be nonzero: if C(q)=0, then A(q)=B(q)C(q)=0, contradicting that A(q) is nonzero.

Now let r=deg(B) and s=deg(C). Since B and C are nonzero, we may write

B(q)=b_r q^r + b_{r-1} q^{r-1}+\cdots+b_0, with b_r\neq 0,
C(q)=c_s q^s + c_{s-1} q^{s-1}+\cdots+c_0, with c_s\neq 0.

In the product B(q)C(q), every term has degree at most r+s, because it comes from multiplying q^i by q^j with i\le r and j\le s. The coefficient of q^{r+s} is b_r c_s, which is nonzero because b_r and c_s are nonzero integers. Therefore the product B(q)C(q) has degree exactly r+s. Hence

deg(A)=deg(B(q)C(q))=r+s=deg(B)+deg(C).

Since C is a nonzero polynomial, deg(C)=s\ge 0. Therefore

deg(A)=deg(B)+deg(C)\ge deg(B).

This proves that deg(A)\ge deg(B).

Assume the hypotheses: n, a, b are integers with 0 <= a, 0 <= b, 2*a <= n, 2*b <= n, and a(n-a) >= b(n-b). We must show a >= b.

Suppose, for contradiction, that a < b. Then a-b < 0. Also, since a < b, we have a+b < 2b, and because 2b <= n, it follows that a+b < n. Hence n-a-b > 0.

Now compute

a(n-a)-b(n-b)
= an-a^2-bn+b^2
= (a-b)n-(a^2-b^2)
= (a-b)n-(a-b)(a+b)
= (a-b)(n-a-b).

But we have shown that a-b < 0 and n-a-b > 0, so their product is negative. Therefore

a(n-a)-b(n-b) = (a-b)(n-a-b) < 0,

which means

a(n-a) < b(n-b).

This contradicts the assumption that a(n-a) >= b(n-b).

Therefore our assumption a < b was impossible, and so a >= b. This proves the statement.

children.proof_nl:
Work in the field of rational functions in q, so that all displayed divisions are legitimate formal operations. Since 0 <= a <= b and a + b <= n, the number r := n - a - b is a nonnegative integer, and
n - a = r + b,    n - b = r + a.
Hence all q-Pochhammer symbols that appear below have nonnegative indices.

By the stated definition of the Gaussian q-binomial coefficient,
([n choose b]_q)/([n choose a]_q)
= ((q;q)_n / ((q;q)_b (q;q)_{n-b})) / ((q;q)_n / ((q;q)_a (q;q)_{n-a}))
= ((q;q)_a (q;q)_{n-a}) / ((q;q)_b (q;q)_{n-b})
= ((q;q)_a (q;q)_{r+b}) / ((q;q)_b (q;q)_{r+a}).

Now use the definition (q;q)_m = product_{j=1}^m (1 - q^j) together with the empty-product convention. Because a <= b,
(q;q)_b = (product_{j=1}^a (1 - q^j)) (product_{j=a+1}^b (1 - q^j))
= (q;q)_a * product_{i=a+1}^b (1 - q^i).
Similarly,
(q;q)_{r+b} = (product_{j=1}^{r+a} (1 - q^j)) (product_{j=r+a+1}^{r+b} (1 - q^j))
= (q;q)_{r+a} * product_{j=r+a+1}^{r+b} (1 - q^j).
Reindex the last product by j = r + i. As i runs from a+1 to b, j runs from r+a+1 to r+b, so
product_{j=r+a+1}^{r+b} (1 - q^j) = product_{i=a+1}^b (1 - q^(r+i)).
Therefore,
(q;q)_{r+b} = (q;q)_{r+a} * product_{i=a+1}^b (1 - q^(r+i)).

Substituting these two factorizations into the earlier expression gives
([n choose b]_q)/([n choose a]_q)
= ((q;q)_a (q;q)_{r+a} * product_{i=a+1}^b (1 - q^(r+i))) / (((q;q)_a * product_{i=a+1}^b (1 - q^i)) (q;q)_{r+a})
= (product_{i=a+1}^b (1 - q^(r+i))) / (product_{i=a+1}^b (1 - q^i))
= product_{i=a+1}^b ((1 - q^(r+i)) / (1 - q^i)).

If a = b, each product from i = a+1 to b is empty, hence equal to 1, and the same computation yields 1 on both sides. Thus the claimed identity holds for all integers n, a, b with 0 <= a <= b and a + b <= n.

children.proof_nl:
If a = b, then the product is empty, so P_{a,b,r}(q) = 1, and for every positive integer d both floor differences are 0. Thus the claim is trivial in this case.

Assume now that a < b. Since (1 - q^(r+i)) / (1 - q^i) = (q^(r+i) - 1) / (q^i - 1) for each i, write
N(q) := product_{i=a+1}^b (q^(r+i) - 1),
D(q) := product_{i=a+1}^b (q^i - 1).
Then P_{a,b,r}(q) = N(q) / D(q). Also D(q) is monic and nonconstant, because each factor q^i - 1 is monic and there is at least one factor.

For a complex number zeta and a polynomial F, let mult_zeta(F) denote the multiplicity of zeta as a root of F.

Fix a positive integer d and let zeta be a primitive d-th root of unity. For any integer m >= 1, zeta is a root of q^m - 1 exactly when d divides m. Moreover that root is simple, because (q^m - 1)' = m q^(m-1), and at zeta this derivative is m zeta^(m-1) != 0. Hence
mult_zeta(q^m - 1) = 1 if d divides m, and 0 otherwise.

Therefore
mult_zeta(D) = #{ i in {a+1,...,b} : d divides i }
              = floor(b/d) - floor(a/d),
because floor(v/d) - floor(u/d) counts the multiples of d in {u+1,...,v}. Likewise,
mult_zeta(N) = #{ i in {a+1,...,b} : d divides (r+i) }
              = #{ m in {r+a+1,...,r+b} : d divides m }
              = floor((r+b)/d) - floor((r+a)/d).

Now suppose first that P_{a,b,r}(q) belongs to Z[q]. Then N = D P_{a,b,r} in C[q]. So for every complex number zeta,
mult_zeta(N) = mult_zeta(D) + mult_zeta(P_{a,b,r}) >= mult_zeta(D).
Applying this to a primitive d-th root of unity gives
floor((r+b)/d) - floor((r+a)/d) >= floor(b/d) - floor(a/d)
for every positive integer d.

Conversely, assume that for every positive integer d,
floor((r+b)/d) - floor((r+a)/d) >= floor(b/d) - floor(a/d).
Let zeta be any complex root of D, and let d be the order of zeta. Then zeta is a primitive d-th root of unity, so the formulas above show that mult_zeta(N) >= mult_zeta(D). Thus every root of D occurs in N with at least the same multiplicity as in D. Since over C polynomials factor into linear factors, this implies that D divides N in C[q].

Because D is monic and N,D are in Z[q], ordinary long division of N by D gives polynomials Q,R in Z[q] with
N = DQ + R,   deg R < deg D.
But D divides N in C[q], and clearly D divides DQ in C[q], so D divides R = N - DQ in C[q]. If R were nonzero, then any polynomial divisible by the nonconstant polynomial D would have degree at least deg D, contradicting deg R < deg D. Hence R = 0. So N = DQ with Q in Z[q]. Therefore
P_{a,b,r}(q) = N(q) / D(q) = Q(q) belongs to Z[q].

This proves the equivalence.

children.proof_nl:
Let n := a + b + r, and for m >= 0 write (q)_m := product_{j=1}^m (1 - q^j). Then
P_{a,b,r}(q) = ((q)_{r+b}/(q)_{r+a}) / ((q)_b/(q)_a) = (q)_{r+b}(q)_a / ((q)_{r+a}(q)_b).
Using the standard formula for Gaussian q-binomial coefficients,
[N choose K]_q = (q)_N / ((q)_K (q)_{N-K}),
we obtain
[n choose b]_q / [n choose a]_q = (q)_a (q)_{n-a} / ((q)_b (q)_{n-b}).
Since n - a = r + b and n - b = r + a, this is exactly
(q)_{r+b}(q)_a / ((q)_{r+a}(q)_b) = P_{a,b,r}(q).
So P_{a,b,r}(q) is a quotient of two Gaussian q-binomial coefficients with the same top n.

Now we prove that this quotient is a polynomial. Fix a positive integer d, and let e_d be the exponent of the cyclotomic polynomial Phi_d(q) in P_{a,b,r}(q). In the product (q)_m = product_{j=1}^m (1 - q^j), the factor Phi_d(q) appears once for each j divisible by d; hence its exponent in (q)_m is floor(m/d). Therefore

e_d = floor((r+b)/d) + floor(a/d) - floor((r+a)/d) - floor(b/d)
    = (floor((r+b)/d) - floor((r+a)/d)) - (floor(b/d) - floor(a/d)).

By the hypothesis, this number is >= 0 for every positive integer d. Also e_d = 0 for d > r+b, so only finitely many e_d are nonzero. Hence

1. lem_20260329073907_5973d29f: For all integers n and r with 0 <= r <= n, if the Gaussian q-binomial coefficient is defined by [n choose r]_q := (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r}), where (q;q)_m := product_{i=1}^m (1 - q^i) and (q;q)_0 := 1, then [n choose r]_q = [n choose n-r]_q as polynomials in q.

Since n-r is an admissible lower index as well, the same definition gives
[n choose n-r]_q = (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_{n-r} (q;q)_{n-(n-r)}) = (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_{n-r} (q;q)_r).

Now multiplication of polynomials is commutative, so
(q;q)_{n-r} (q;q)_r = (q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r}.
Therefore the two right-hand sides are identical, and hence
[n choose n-r]_q = (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r}) = [n choose r]_q.

Thus [n choose r]_q = [n choose n-r]_q. Since both sides are the Gaussian q-binomial coefficients defined by the given q-factorial formula, this is an identity of polynomials in q. This proves the claimed symmetry.

2. lem_20260329073914_bfaa8c0e: For all integers n and r with 0 <= r <= n, the Gaussian q-binomial coefficient [n choose r]_q := (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r}), where (q;q)_m := product_{i=1}^m (1 - q^i) and (q;q)_0 := 1, is a nonzero polynomial in Z[q] of degree r(n-r).
Let G_{n,r}(q) := (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r}). Since each factor 1 - q^i is a nonzero polynomial in Z[q], each (q;q)_m is nonzero, so G_{n,r}(q) is a well-defined element of the rational function field Q(q).

We prove by induction on n that for every integer r with 0 <= r <= n, G_{n,r}(q) is a nonzero polynomial in Z[q] of degree r(n-r).

Base case n = 0: then r = 0, and
G_{0,0}(q) = (q;q)_0 / ((q;q)_0 (q;q)_0) = 1.
This is a nonzero polynomial in Z[q] of degree 0 = 0(0-0).

Induction step: assume the claim has been proved for n-1, and let r satisfy 0 <= r <= n.

If r = 0, then
G_{n,0}(q) = (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_0 (q;q)_n) = 1.
If r = n, then
G_{n,n}(q) = (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_n (q;q)_0) = 1.
In either case G_{n,r}(q) is a nonzero polynomial of degree 0 = r(n-r).

Now assume 0 < r < n. We derive the usual recurrence directly from the definition. Using
(q;q)_{n-r} = (1 - q^{n-r})(q;q)_{n-r-1}
and
(q;q)_r = (1 - q^r)(q;q)_{r-1},
we have in Q(q):

G_{n-1,r}(q)
= (q;q)_{n-1} / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r-1})
= (1 - q^{n-r})(q;q)_{n-1} / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r}),

and

q^{n-r} G_{n-1,r-1}(q)
= q^{n-r} (q;q)_{n-1} / ((q;q)_{r-1} (q;q)_{n-r})
= q^{n-r}(1 - q^r)(q;q)_{n-1} / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r}).

Adding these two identities gives

G_{n-1,r}(q) + q^{n-r} G_{n-1,r-1}(q)
= ((1 - q^{n-r}) + q^{n-r}(1 - q^r))(q;q)_{n-1} / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r})
= (1 - q^n)(q;q)_{n-1} / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r})
= (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r})
= G_{n,r}(q).

So for 0 < r < n,
G_{n,r}(q) = G_{n-1,r}(q) + q^{n-r} G_{n-1,r-1}(q).

By the induction hypothesis, both G_{n-1,r}(q) and G_{n-1,r-1}(q) are nonzero polynomials in Z[q]. Hence their sum G_{n,r}(q) also lies in Z[q].

Now compute degrees. By induction,
deg G_{n-1,r}(q) = r((n-1)-r) = r(n-r) - r,
and
deg G_{n-1,r-1}(q) = (r-1)(n-r).
Therefore

deg(q^{n-r} G_{n-1,r-1}(q)) = (n-r) + (r-1)(n-r) = r(n-r).

Since r > 0, we have
r(n-r) - r < r(n-r).
Thus the second summand has strictly larger degree than the first. Because G_{n-1,r-1}(q) is nonzero, q^{n-r} G_{n-1,r-1}(q) has a nonzero term of degree r(n-r); the first summand has no term of that degree, so no cancellation is possible. Hence

deg G_{n,r}(q) = r(n-r).
In particular G_{n,r}(q) is nonzero.

This completes the induction. Therefore for all integers n and r with 0 <= r <= n, the Gaussian q-binomial coefficient [n choose r]_q is a nonzero polynomial in Z[q] of degree r(n-r).

3. lem_20260329073927_1b122a3f: Let A(q) and B(q) be nonzero polynomials in Z[q]. If the rational function A(q) / B(q) is itself a polynomial in Z[q], then deg(A) >= deg(B).
Assume that the rational function A(q)/B(q) is a polynomial in Z[q]. Then there exists a polynomial C(q) in Z[q] such that

A(q)=B(q)C(q).

Because A(q) and B(q) are both nonzero, C(q) must also be nonzero: if C(q)=0, then A(q)=B(q)C(q)=0, contradicting that A(q) is nonzero.

Now let r=deg(B) and s=deg(C). Since B and C are nonzero, we may write

B(q)=b_r q^r + b_{r-1} q^{r-1}+\cdots+b_0, with b_r\neq 0,
C(q)=c_s q^s + c_{s-1} q^{s-1}+\cdots+c_0, with c_s\neq 0.

In the product B(q)C(q), every term has degree at most r+s, because it comes from multiplying q^i by q^j with i\le r and j\le s. The coefficient of q^{r+s} is b_r c_s, which is nonzero because b_r and c_s are nonzero integers. Therefore the product B(q)C(q) has degree exactly r+s. Hence

deg(A)=deg(B(q)C(q))=r+s=deg(B)+deg(C).

Since C is a nonzero polynomial, deg(C)=s\ge 0. Therefore

deg(A)=deg(B)+deg(C)\ge deg(B).

This proves that deg(A)\ge deg(B).

Assume the hypotheses: n, a, b are integers with 0 <= a, 0 <= b, 2*a <= n, 2*b <= n, and a(n-a) >= b(n-b). We must show a >= b.

Suppose, for contradiction, that a < b. Then a-b < 0. Also, since a < b, we have a+b < 2b, and because 2b <= n, it follows that a+b < n. Hence n-a-b > 0.

Now compute

a(n-a)-b(n-b)
= an-a^2-bn+b^2
= (a-b)n-(a^2-b^2)
= (a-b)n-(a-b)(a+b)
= (a-b)(n-a-b).

But we have shown that a-b < 0 and n-a-b > 0, so their product is negative. Therefore

a(n-a)-b(n-b) = (a-b)(n-a-b) < 0,

which means

a(n-a) < b(n-b).

This contradicts the assumption that a(n-a) >= b(n-b).

Therefore our assumption a < b was impossible, and so a >= b. This proves the statement.

5. lem_20260329073944_4658f3a6: For integers n, a, b with 0 <= a <= b and a + b <= n, define r := n - a - b. = ((q;q)_a (q;q)_{n-a}) / ((q;q)_b (q;q)_{n-b})

(q;q)_b = (product_{j=1}^a (1 - q^j)) (product_{j=a+1}^b (1 - q^j))

Similarly,
(q;q)_{r+b} = (product_{j=1}^{r+a} (1 - q^j)) (product_{j=r+a+1}^{r+b} (1 - q^j))

([n choose b]_q)/([n choose a]_q)
= ((q;q)_a (q;q)_{r+a} * product_{i=a+1}^b (1 - q^(r+i))) / (((q;q)_a * product_{i=a+1}^b (1 - q^i)) (q;q)_{r+a})

If a = b, each product from i = a+1 to b is empty, hence equal to 1, and the same computation yields 1 on both sides. Thus the claimed identity holds for all integers n, a, b with 0 <= a <= b and a + b <= n.

6. lem_20260329074006_a15c13f0: Let a, b, r be integers with 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0. Define P_{a,b,r}(q) := product_{i=a+1}^{b} ((1 - q^(r+i)) / (1 - q^i)), with empty product equal to 1. Assume now that a < b. Since (1 - q^(r+i)) / (1 - q^i) = (q^(r+i) - 1) / (q^i - 1) for each i, write
N(q) := product_{i=a+1}^b (q^(r+i) - 1),
D(q) := product_{i=a+1}^b (q^i - 1).
Then P_{a,b,r}(q) = N(q) / D(q). Also D(q) is monic and nonconstant, because each factor q^i - 1 is monic and there is at least one factor.

For a complex number zeta and a polynomial F, let mult_zeta(F) denote the multiplicity of zeta as a root of F.

Fix a positive integer d and let zeta be a primitive d-th root of unity. For any integer m >= 1, zeta is a root of q^m - 1 exactly when d divides m. Moreover that root is simple, because (q^m - 1)' = m q^(m-1), and at zeta this derivative is m zeta^(m-1) != 0. Hence
mult_zeta(q^m - 1) = 1 if d divides m, and 0 otherwise.

Therefore
mult_zeta(D) = #{ i in {a+1,...,b} : d divides i }
              = floor(b/d) - floor(a/d),
because floor(v/d) - floor(u/d) counts the multiples of d in {u+1,...,v}. Likewise,
mult_zeta(N) = #{ i in {a+1,...,b} : d divides (r+i) }
              = #{ m in {r+a+1,...,r+b} : d divides m }
              = floor((r+b)/d) - floor((r+a)/d).

mult_zeta(N) = mult_zeta(D) + mult_zeta(P_{a,b,r}) >= mult_zeta(D).
Applying this to a primitive d-th root of unity gives
floor((r+b)/d) - floor((r+a)/d) >= floor(b/d) - floor(a/d)
for every positive integer d.

Conversely, assume that for every positive integer d,
floor((r+b)/d) - floor((r+a)/d) >= floor(b/d) - floor(a/d).

Because D is monic and N,D are in Z[q], ordinary long division of N by D gives polynomials Q,R in Z[q] with
N = DQ + R,   deg R < deg D.
But D divides N in C[q], and clearly D divides DQ in C[q], so D divides R = N - DQ in C[q]. If R were nonzero, then any polynomial divisible by the nonconstant polynomial D would have degree at least deg D, contradicting deg R < deg D. Hence R = 0. So N = DQ with Q in Z[q]. Therefore
P_{a,b,r}(q) = N(q) / D(q) = Q(q) belongs to Z[q].

This proves the equivalence.

7. lem_20260329074016_d9949d95: Let a, b, r be integers with 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0. Define P_{a,b,r}(q) := product_{i=a+1}^{b} ((1 - q^(r+i)) / (1 - q^i)), with empty product equal to 1. P_{a,b,r}(q) = ((q)_{r+b}/(q)_{r+a}) / ((q)_b/(q)_a) = (q)_{r+b}(q)_a / ((q)_{r+a}(q)_b).
Using the standard formula for Gaussian q-binomial coefficients,
[N choose K]_q = (q)_N / ((q)_K (q)_{N-K}),

Since n - a = r + b and n - b = r + a, this is exactly

By the hypothesis, this number is >= 0 for every positive integer d. Also e_d = 0 for d > r+b, so only finitely many e_d are nonzero. Hence

is a polynomial in q. Applying the allowed dependency root_semantic_sketch with k = b and l = a, we conclude that every coefficient of this polynomial is nonnegative. Therefore P_{a,b,r}(q) is a polynomial in Z[q], and all of its coefficients are at least 0.

Assembly skeleton: Fix integers n, k, l with 0 <= k, l <= n and assume that [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q is a polynomial. First use the symmetry [n choose r]_q = [n choose n-r]_q to replace k and l by k' = min(k, n-k) and l' = min(l, n-l); this leaves the quotient unchanged and puts both indices in the first half of [0,n]. Since the reduced quotient is still a polynomial, a general degree argument shows that the degree of its numerator is at least the degree of its denominator. Using deg([n choose r]_q) = r(n-r), this becomes k'(n-k') >= l'(n-l'). On the first half of the interval, the quadratic r(n-r) is increasing, so k' >= l'. Writing a = l', b = k', and r = n-a-b, the reduced quotient becomes the shifted interval q-factorial ratio product_{i=a+1}^{b} ((1 - q^(r+i)) / (1 - q^i)). Cyclotomic counting then turns the assumption that this product is a polynomial into the floor inequalities floor((r+b)/d) - floor((r+a)/d) >= floor(b/d) - floor(a/d) for every positive integer d. The bottleneck lemma asserts that any shifted interval product satisfying those inequalities has nonnegative coefficients. Applying that lemma to the reduced quotient and then substituting back yields the original theorem.

Recursive lemma proofs:

1. lem_20260329073907_5973d29f: For all integers n and r with 0 <= r <= n, if the Gaussian q-binomial coefficient is defined by [n choose r]_q := (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r}), where (q;q)_m := product_{i=1}^m (1 - q^i) and (q;q)_0 := 1, then [n choose r]_q = [n choose n-r]_q as polynomials in q.
Fix integers n and r with 0 <= r <= n. Then n-r is also an integer, and 0 <= n-r <= n.

By the stated definition,
[n choose r]_q = (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r}).

Since n-r is an admissible lower index as well, the same definition gives
[n choose n-r]_q = (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_{n-r} (q;q)_{n-(n-r)}) = (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_{n-r} (q;q)_r).

Now multiplication of polynomials is commutative, so
(q;q)_{n-r} (q;q)_r = (q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r}.
Therefore the two right-hand sides are identical, and hence
[n choose n-r]_q = (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r}) = [n choose r]_q.

Thus [n choose r]_q = [n choose n-r]_q. Since both sides are the Gaussian q-binomial coefficients defined by the given q-factorial formula, this is an identity of polynomials in q. This proves the claimed symmetry.

2. lem_20260329073914_bfaa8c0e: For all integers n and r with 0 <= r <= n, the Gaussian q-binomial coefficient [n choose r]_q := (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r}), where (q;q)_m := product_{i=1}^m (1 - q^i) and (q;q)_0 := 1, is a nonzero polynomial in Z[q] of degree r(n-r).
Let G_{n,r}(q) := (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r}). Since each factor 1 - q^i is a nonzero polynomial in Z[q], each (q;q)_m is nonzero, so G_{n,r}(q) is a well-defined element of the rational function field Q(q).

We prove by induction on n that for every integer r with 0 <= r <= n, G_{n,r}(q) is a nonzero polynomial in Z[q] of degree r(n-r).

Base case n = 0: then r = 0, and
G_{0,0}(q) = (q;q)_0 / ((q;q)_0 (q;q)_0) = 1.
This is a nonzero polynomial in Z[q] of degree 0 = 0(0-0).

Induction step: assume the claim has been proved for n-1, and let r satisfy 0 <= r <= n.

If r = 0, then
G_{n,0}(q) = (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_0 (q;q)_n) = 1.
If r = n, then
G_{n,n}(q) = (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_n (q;q)_0) = 1.
In either case G_{n,r}(q) is a nonzero polynomial of degree 0 = r(n-r).

Now assume 0 < r < n. We derive the usual recurrence directly from the definition. Using
(q;q)_{n-r} = (1 - q^{n-r})(q;q)_{n-r-1}
and
(q;q)_r = (1 - q^r)(q;q)_{r-1},
we have in Q(q):

G_{n-1,r}(q)
= (q;q)_{n-1} / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r-1})
= (1 - q^{n-r})(q;q)_{n-1} / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r}),

and

q^{n-r} G_{n-1,r-1}(q)
= q^{n-r} (q;q)_{n-1} / ((q;q)_{r-1} (q;q)_{n-r})
= q^{n-r}(1 - q^r)(q;q)_{n-1} / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r}).

Adding these two identities gives

G_{n-1,r}(q) + q^{n-r} G_{n-1,r-1}(q)
= ((1 - q^{n-r}) + q^{n-r}(1 - q^r))(q;q)_{n-1} / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r})
= (1 - q^n)(q;q)_{n-1} / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r})
= (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r})
= G_{n,r}(q).

So for 0 < r < n,
G_{n,r}(q) = G_{n-1,r}(q) + q^{n-r} G_{n-1,r-1}(q).

By the induction hypothesis, both G_{n-1,r}(q) and G_{n-1,r-1}(q) are nonzero polynomials in Z[q]. Hence their sum G_{n,r}(q) also lies in Z[q].

Now compute degrees. By induction,
deg G_{n-1,r}(q) = r((n-1)-r) = r(n-r) - r,
and
deg G_{n-1,r-1}(q) = (r-1)(n-r).
Therefore

deg(q^{n-r} G_{n-1,r-1}(q)) = (n-r) + (r-1)(n-r) = r(n-r).

Since r > 0, we have
r(n-r) - r < r(n-r).
Thus the second summand has strictly larger degree than the first. Because G_{n-1,r-1}(q) is nonzero, q^{n-r} G_{n-1,r-1}(q) has a nonzero term of degree r(n-r); the first summand has no term of that degree, so no cancellation is possible. Hence

deg G_{n,r}(q) = r(n-r).
In particular G_{n,r}(q) is nonzero.

This completes the induction. Therefore for all integers n and r with 0 <= r <= n, the Gaussian q-binomial coefficient [n choose r]_q is a nonzero polynomial in Z[q] of degree r(n-r).

3. lem_20260329073927_1b122a3f: Let A(q) and B(q) be nonzero polynomials in Z[q]. If the rational function A(q) / B(q) is itself a polynomial in Z[q], then deg(A) >= deg(B).
Assume that the rational function A(q)/B(q) is a polynomial in Z[q]. Then there exists a polynomial C(q) in Z[q] such that

A(q)=B(q)C(q).

Because A(q) and B(q) are both nonzero, C(q) must also be nonzero: if C(q)=0, then A(q)=B(q)C(q)=0, contradicting that A(q) is nonzero.

Now let r=deg(B) and s=deg(C). Since B and C are nonzero, we may write

B(q)=b_r q^r + b_{r-1} q^{r-1}+\cdots+b_0, with b_r\neq 0,
C(q)=c_s q^s + c_{s-1} q^{s-1}+\cdots+c_0, with c_s\neq 0.

In the product B(q)C(q), every term has degree at most r+s, because it comes from multiplying q^i by q^j with i\le r and j\le s. The coefficient of q^{r+s} is b_r c_s, which is nonzero because b_r and c_s are nonzero integers. Therefore the product B(q)C(q) has degree exactly r+s. Hence

deg(A)=deg(B(q)C(q))=r+s=deg(B)+deg(C).

Since C is a nonzero polynomial, deg(C)=s\ge 0. Therefore

deg(A)=deg(B)+deg(C)\ge deg(B).

This proves that deg(A)\ge deg(B).

4. lem_20260329073933_51291146: For all integers n, a, b with 0 <= a, 0 <= b, 2*a <= n, and 2*b <= n, if a(n-a) >= b(n-b), then a >= b.
Assume the hypotheses: n, a, b are integers with 0 <= a, 0 <= b, 2*a <= n, 2*b <= n, and a(n-a) >= b(n-b). We must show a >= b.

Suppose, for contradiction, that a < b. Then a-b < 0. Also, since a < b, we have a+b < 2b, and because 2b <= n, it follows that a+b < n. Hence n-a-b > 0.

Now compute

a(n-a)-b(n-b)
= an-a^2-bn+b^2
= (a-b)n-(a^2-b^2)
= (a-b)n-(a-b)(a+b)
= (a-b)(n-a-b).

But we have shown that a-b < 0 and n-a-b > 0, so their product is negative. Therefore

a(n-a)-b(n-b) = (a-b)(n-a-b) < 0,

which means

a(n-a) < b(n-b).

This contradicts the assumption that a(n-a) >= b(n-b).

Therefore our assumption a < b was impossible, and so a >= b. This proves the statement.

5. lem_20260329073944_4658f3a6: For integers n, a, b with 0 <= a <= b and a + b <= n, define r := n - a - b. Then the quotient of Gaussian q-binomial coefficients satisfies [n choose b]_q / [n choose a]_q = product_{i=a+1}^{b} ((1 - q^(r+i)) / (1 - q^i)), where [n choose t]_q := (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_t (q;q)_{n-t}), (q;q)_m := product_{j=1}^m (1 - q^j), (q;q)_0 := 1, and an empty product is interpreted as 1.
Work in the field of rational functions in q, so that all displayed divisions are legitimate formal operations. Since 0 <= a <= b and a + b <= n, the number r := n - a - b is a nonnegative integer, and
n - a = r + b,    n - b = r + a.
Hence all q-Pochhammer symbols that appear below have nonnegative indices.

By the stated definition of the Gaussian q-binomial coefficient,
([n choose b]_q)/([n choose a]_q)
= ((q;q)_n / ((q;q)_b (q;q)_{n-b})) / ((q;q)_n / ((q;q)_a (q;q)_{n-a}))
= ((q;q)_a (q;q)_{n-a}) / ((q;q)_b (q;q)_{n-b})
= ((q;q)_a (q;q)_{r+b}) / ((q;q)_b (q;q)_{r+a}).

Now use the definition (q;q)_m = product_{j=1}^m (1 - q^j) together with the empty-product convention. Because a <= b,
(q;q)_b = (product_{j=1}^a (1 - q^j)) (product_{j=a+1}^b (1 - q^j))
= (q;q)_a * product_{i=a+1}^b (1 - q^i).
Similarly,
(q;q)_{r+b} = (product_{j=1}^{r+a} (1 - q^j)) (product_{j=r+a+1}^{r+b} (1 - q^j))
= (q;q)_{r+a} * product_{j=r+a+1}^{r+b} (1 - q^j).
Reindex the last product by j = r + i. As i runs from a+1 to b, j runs from r+a+1 to r+b, so
product_{j=r+a+1}^{r+b} (1 - q^j) = product_{i=a+1}^b (1 - q^(r+i)).
Therefore,
(q;q)_{r+b} = (q;q)_{r+a} * product_{i=a+1}^b (1 - q^(r+i)).

Substituting these two factorizations into the earlier expression gives
([n choose b]_q)/([n choose a]_q)
= ((q;q)_a (q;q)_{r+a} * product_{i=a+1}^b (1 - q^(r+i))) / (((q;q)_a * product_{i=a+1}^b (1 - q^i)) (q;q)_{r+a})
= (product_{i=a+1}^b (1 - q^(r+i))) / (product_{i=a+1}^b (1 - q^i))
= product_{i=a+1}^b ((1 - q^(r+i)) / (1 - q^i)).

If a = b, each product from i = a+1 to b is empty, hence equal to 1, and the same computation yields 1 on both sides. Thus the claimed identity holds for all integers n, a, b with 0 <= a <= b and a + b <= n.

6. lem_20260329074006_a15c13f0: Let a, b, r be integers with 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0. Define P_{a,b,r}(q) := product_{i=a+1}^{b} ((1 - q^(r+i)) / (1 - q^i)), with empty product equal to 1. Then P_{a,b,r}(q) belongs to Z[q] if and only if for every positive integer d one has floor((r+b)/d) - floor((r+a)/d) >= floor(b/d) - floor(a/d).
If a = b, then the product is empty, so P_{a,b,r}(q) = 1, and for every positive integer d both floor differences are 0. Thus the claim is trivial in this case.

Assume now that a < b. Since (1 - q^(r+i)) / (1 - q^i) = (q^(r+i) - 1) / (q^i - 1) for each i, write
N(q) := product_{i=a+1}^b (q^(r+i) - 1),
D(q) := product_{i=a+1}^b (q^i - 1).
Then P_{a,b,r}(q) = N(q) / D(q). Also D(q) is monic and nonconstant, because each factor q^i - 1 is monic and there is at least one factor.

For a complex number zeta and a polynomial F, let mult_zeta(F) denote the multiplicity of zeta as a root of F.

Fix a positive integer d and let zeta be a primitive d-th root of unity. For any integer m >= 1, zeta is a root of q^m - 1 exactly when d divides m. Moreover that root is simple, because (q^m - 1)' = m q^(m-1), and at zeta this derivative is m zeta^(m-1) != 0. Hence
mult_zeta(q^m - 1) = 1 if d divides m, and 0 otherwise.

Therefore
mult_zeta(D) = #{ i in {a+1,...,b} : d divides i }
              = floor(b/d) - floor(a/d),
because floor(v/d) - floor(u/d) counts the multiples of d in {u+1,...,v}. Likewise,
mult_zeta(N) = #{ i in {a+1,...,b} : d divides (r+i) }
              = #{ m in {r+a+1,...,r+b} : d divides m }
              = floor((r+b)/d) - floor((r+a)/d).

Now suppose first that P_{a,b,r}(q) belongs to Z[q]. Then N = D P_{a,b,r} in C[q]. So for every complex number zeta,
mult_zeta(N) = mult_zeta(D) + mult_zeta(P_{a,b,r}) >= mult_zeta(D).
Applying this to a primitive d-th root of unity gives
floor((r+b)/d) - floor((r+a)/d) >= floor(b/d) - floor(a/d)
for every positive integer d.

Conversely, assume that for every positive integer d,
floor((r+b)/d) - floor((r+a)/d) >= floor(b/d) - floor(a/d).
Let zeta be any complex root of D, and let d be the order of zeta. Then zeta is a primitive d-th root of unity, so the formulas above show that mult_zeta(N) >= mult_zeta(D). Thus every root of D occurs in N with at least the same multiplicity as in D. Since over C polynomials factor into linear factors, this implies that D divides N in C[q].

Because D is monic and N,D are in Z[q], ordinary long division of N by D gives polynomials Q,R in Z[q] with
N = DQ + R,   deg R < deg D.
But D divides N in C[q], and clearly D divides DQ in C[q], so D divides R = N - DQ in C[q]. If R were nonzero, then any polynomial divisible by the nonconstant polynomial D would have degree at least deg D, contradicting deg R < deg D. Hence R = 0. So N = DQ with Q in Z[q]. Therefore
P_{a,b,r}(q) = N(q) / D(q) = Q(q) belongs to Z[q].

This proves the equivalence.

7. lem_20260329074016_d9949d95: Let a, b, r be integers with 0 <= a <= b and r >= 0. Define P_{a,b,r}(q) := product_{i=a+1}^{b} ((1 - q^(r+i)) / (1 - q^i)), with empty product equal to 1. Assume that for every positive integer d one has floor((r+b)/d) - floor((r+a)/d) >= floor(b/d) - floor(a/d). Then P_{a,b,r}(q) is a polynomial in Z[q], and every coefficient of P_{a,b,r}(q) is nonnegative.
Let n := a + b + r, and for m >= 0 write (q)_m := product_{j=1}^m (1 - q^j). Then
P_{a,b,r}(q) = ((q)_{r+b}/(q)_{r+a}) / ((q)_b/(q)_a) = (q)_{r+b}(q)_a / ((q)_{r+a}(q)_b).
Using the standard formula for Gaussian q-binomial coefficients,
[N choose K]_q = (q)_N / ((q)_K (q)_{N-K}),
we obtain
[n choose b]_q / [n choose a]_q = (q)_a (q)_{n-a} / ((q)_b (q)_{n-b}).
Since n - a = r + b and n - b = r + a, this is exactly
(q)_{r+b}(q)_a / ((q)_{r+a}(q)_b) = P_{a,b,r}(q).
So P_{a,b,r}(q) is a quotient of two Gaussian q-binomial coefficients with the same top n.

Now we prove that this quotient is a polynomial. Fix a positive integer d, and let e_d be the exponent of the cyclotomic polynomial Phi_d(q) in P_{a,b,r}(q). In the product (q)_m = product_{j=1}^m (1 - q^j), the factor Phi_d(q) appears once for each j divisible by d; hence its exponent in (q)_m is floor(m/d). Therefore

e_d = floor((r+b)/d) + floor(a/d) - floor((r+a)/d) - floor(b/d)
    = (floor((r+b)/d) - floor((r+a)/d)) - (floor(b/d) - floor(a/d)).

By the hypothesis, this number is >= 0 for every positive integer d. Also e_d = 0 for d > r+b, so only finitely many e_d are nonzero. Hence
P_{a,b,r}(q) = product_{d >= 1} Phi_d(q)^{e_d}
belongs to Z[q].

Finally, 0 <= a <= b <= n, and we have shown that
P_{a,b,r}(q) = [n choose b]_q / [n choose a]_q
is a polynomial in q. Applying the allowed dependency root_semantic_sketch with k = b and l = a, we conclude that every coefficient of this polynomial is nonnegative. Therefore P_{a,b,r}(q) is a polynomial in Z[q], and all of its coefficients are at least 0.
